item.title: Shiga's Sake Breweries: Lake Water, Mountain Rice — Guide
item.description: Shiga is one of Japan’s quietly excellent sake regions: more than 30 breweries work the prefecture, drawing soft water filtered through the mountains of the Lake Biwa watershed and rice from the fertile Omi plain, producing sake known for gentle umami depth that pairs naturally with the lake’s cuisine. Historic kura cluster around Otsu — where the brewery quarter near the old Tokaido road keeps its earthen storehouses — and in merchant towns like Hino and Harie, whose springs run so pure that households channel them through their kitchens, and many breweries open their doors for tastings, tours and seasonal fresh-pressed namazake.

item.title: Takayama Sanmachi Suji: A Beautifully Preserved Merchant Old Town — Guide
item.description: Sanmachi Suji is the beautifully preserved heart of Takayama’s old town, a cluster of narrow lanes lined with dark wooden merchant houses dating from the Edo period, when the town prospered as a centre of skilled carpenters and merchants in the mountainous Hida region. Today the lanes are home to sake breweries marked by cedar-ball signs, cafes, craft shops, and stalls selling Hida beef and local sweets, making it one of Japan’s most atmospheric and enjoyable historic districts to explore on foot.

item.title: Niigata Hidden Gems: Matsunoyama, Sado's Remote Villages & Snow Country Backroads
item.description: Hidden Gems of Niigata Prefecture: A Traveler’s Guide to Japan’s Most Overlooked Region Niigata Prefecture remains a mystery to most foreign visitors—a snow-covered enigma on the Japan Sea coast known vaguely for rice, sake, and ski resorts. Yet this very obscurity has preserved some of Japan’s most authentic experiences. While the Golden Route tourists speed past on the Shinkansen toward Kyoto, Niigata’s back roads, mountain valleys, and coastal villages hold treasures that reward the curious traveler willing to venture off-piste.
